summary: On a long mission the crew are the first, and sometimes the only, people who can notice a change in their own health. Astronaut Health Monitor is a visual self-assessment tool for that moment. A crew member records a short daily check-in, sees on a body map which body region or cabin reading needs attention, and is told in plain words what to do and when to involve the crew medical officer or the flight surgeon. Readings are judged against NASA-STD-3001 limits and published clinical ranges, radiation dose is projected against NASA's 600 mSv career limit, and NASA's live space-weather feed raises a solar particle event alert. The app works with no connection and words its guidance for the mission's communication delay, from near real time on the station to forty minutes for a reply at Mars. Crew readings are simulated and labelled as such; the limits and guidance are NASA's.
details:
What it does. Astronaut Health Monitor has six screens. The Body map shows a figure with seven selectable regions (head, eyes, heart, gut, bones and muscles, whole body, cabin), each marked OK, Watch or Act now. Selecting one shows the reading, how it compares with the crew member's own 14-day average, why it matters in space, numbered steps to take, and who to tell. The Check-in guides the entry of blood pressure, heart rate, fasting blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood, vision, cabin CO2 and cabin temperature, with instructions for each measurement. Trends shows one chart at a time against the healthy range, including a bone-loss estimate and a radiation dose projection. Alerts lists everything that needs attention by urgency, shows live space weather, and builds a report for ground. Routine lists the day's health tasks with a streak and a weekly ring. Hazards links NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight to the readings the app tracks.

Benefits and impact. The crew can spot a change early and act on it without waiting for the ground. Four mission profiles (ISS, lunar surface, Mars transit, Mars surface) change gravity, radiation dose rate and the reply delay, and the guidance is worded for that delay. The record stays on the device, works offline and exports as a CSV file.

How it works. A static website in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no server and no build step. Chart.js draws the charts. The health rules are separate modules covered by 46 automated tests. A service worker lets the app reload with no connection. Live space weather comes from NASA DONKI.

Creativity. The body map is the entry point, the guidance changes with the mission's communication delay, and live space weather is tied to a personal radiation status.

What we considered. Crew readings are simulated because real astronaut medical data is not public, and the app says so on every screen. The limits and rates are NASA's and every source is listed in the README; where a cut-off is our own rule, the app says so. Status is never shown by colour alone. The app is decision support and does not diagnose.

Use of AI. The idea, scope and decisions are ours. The code and documents were written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic) and reviewed by the team. The slides were prepared with Claude assistance. The app uses no AI-generated imagery and does not call an AI model. No NASA logos or branding are used.
